_comment: Structures across verses and chapters, shown from Deep behind the commentary notice: bookends (inclusio), refrains, two threads taking turns (alternation), mirrors (chiasm) and foils (two people set side by side, whose sides may hold several ranges across chapters and books). Checked by crates/atlas-cli/src/extra_structure.rs.

members are the passage's parts in reading order, each with its mark (A and A' for bookends, R for a refrain, A B A B for turns, A B B' A' for a mirror) and its exact BSB words from one verse of its ref; tie, on the first member of each group that answers one another, is words found in every member of the group.

cites follow config/figure-forms.json: only its quotable works are quoted, the cite list in config/layer-sources.json says who wrote each book's words, and strength is the number of different interpreters cited (3 or more widely agreed, 2 commonly held, 1 some interpreters). docs/evidence/structures-2026-11-01.json records where each quote was read.

kinds.label: Bookends
kinds.about: A passage opens and closes with the same words, so the end takes the reader back to the start.

kinds.label: A refrain
kinds.about: The same words come back at set places, like the chorus of a song.

kinds.label: Taking turns
kinds.about: The account moves back and forth between two threads, so each shows up the other.

kinds.label: A mirror
kinds.about: The parts come in one order and then in reverse, A B then B A, often with the turn at the centre.

kinds.label: Set side by side
kinds.about: Two people, often chapters or books apart, are set side by side, and each shows up the other.

structures.evidence: Barnes: the same burden or refrain marks the parts, at 42:5, 42:11 and 43:5. Henry: the fifth verse of Psalm 43 is the same as the eleventh of Psalm 42. Lowth: the psalm should perhaps not be parted from the one before it; if so, the whole has three nearly equal parts, each closed by the same stanza.
structures.limit: Writers differ on whether Psalms 42 and 43 were first written as one psalm; the refrain is in both either way.

cites.quote: Psa 42:1-11 consists of two parts, marked by the "burden" or "refrain" in Psa 42:5, Psa 42:11; and if Psa 43:1-5 were regarded as a part of the same composition, the two would be divided into three parts, marked by the same burden or refrain, in Psa 42:5, Psa 42:11; Psa 43:5.

Though his children prove unfaithful, v. 30. Yet will not God prove unfaithful, v. 35. Though they break God's statutes, v. 31. Yet will not God break his covenant, v. 34. In v. 32, God's chastening in measure is made to correspond with (v. 33)

structures.short: Love and calling, then calling and love

structures.evidence: Forbes: of the two things in verse 28, the second, God's purpose, is enlarged on first, in verses 29 to 34, and the first is then taken up in verses 35 to 39, so that the whole passage forms an epanodos, or introverted parallelism, in which the Christian's love to God has the first and last place.

cites.quote: The second of these ... is first enlarged upon in verses 29-34 (B); and the first is then taken up in verses 35-39 (A): so that the whole passage forms an Epanodos, or Introverted Parallelism, in which the Christian's love to God occupies the first and last place. After the statement of the general proposition in ver. 28, the Apostle first enlarges on the 'purpose' of God in vv. 29-34 (B).

structures.short: Noah's sons named, then their families in reverse
structures.about: The first verse names Shem, Ham and Japheth. The lists of their families then go the other way: Japheth's sons come first and Shem's last, with Ham's between.

members.words: Shem
Ham
and Japheth

The sons of Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.

structures.evidence: Boys: the order is inverted, so Shem and his descendants stand in a and a, Ham and his in b and b, Japheth and his in c and c. Forbes: Shem is placed first and last to mark the pre-eminence God designed for him as forefather of the chosen people. Bullinger lists it under epanodos, words repeated backward. Keil: verse 1 names the sons by age, but the genealogy puts Japheth first and Shem last.

cites.quote: he inverts that order. The sons of Japheth come first, then the sons of Ham, and, last of all, the sons of Shem ... Thus we have Shem and his descendants in a. and a., Ham and his descendants in b. and b., Japheth and his descendants in c. and c.

cites.quote: The reason of this arrangement, however, Mr Boys has omitted to notice. Why should Shem be placed either first or last ... The intention of the sacred historian evidently was to mark the pre-eminence which God designed for Shem in his generations, as the progenitor of the chosen people

structures.short: What he will do and shun, then do and shun again
structures.about: The psalm is the psalmist's resolve throughout. Verses 1 and 2, and again verse 6, tell what he will do and whom he will welcome; verses 3 to 5, and again 7 and 8, what he will shun and whom he will cut off.

members.words: I will ponder the way that is blameless
I will set no worthless thing before my eyes.
he who walks in the way of integrity shall minister to me.
no one who tells lies shall stand in my presence.

structures.evidence: Boys reads the whole psalm as the psalmist's resolutions in four members, the first answering the third and the second the fourth: in the first and third he says what he will do and whom he will encourage, in the second and fourth what he will avoid and whom he will discourage and destroy.

cites.quote: The whole of this Psalm is a promise, or a declaration of the Psalmist's resolutions and intentions. There is, however, a distinction of an obvious kind. In A. and A., the first and third members, the Psalmist sets forth what he will do, and whom he will encourage … in B. and B., the second and fourth, what he will avoid, and whom he will discourage and destroy.

structures.short: Spoken of, then spoken to, twice over
structures.about: Verses 1 and 4 speak of the man who fears the LORD and declare him blessed. Verses 2 and 3, and again 5 and 6, speak to him and tell what the blessing will be.

members.words: Blessed are all who fear the LORD,
For when you eat the fruit of your labor,
In this way indeed shall blessing come to the man who fears the LORD.
May the LORD bless you from Zion,

structures.evidence: Boys calls the psalm an alternate parallelism of four members, the third answering the first and the fourth the second: in the first and third the man is spoken of, in the second and fourth he is spoken to, and the blessing is set out in detail.

cites.quote: In this Psalm we have an alternate parallelism of four members, A., B., A., B.: the third member, A., answering to the first, A.; and the fourth, B., to the second, B. … In A. and A., the first and third members, the man … is spoken of; in B. and B., the second and fourth, he is spoken to. … But in the second and fourth members, B. and B., the nature of the blessing is particularized.
cites.read: the 1825 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/akeytobookpsalm00boysgoog

structures.short: He prays for himself at both ends, about others between
structures.about: The psalm is a prayer throughout. In the first and last verses the psalmist prays for himself and asks for help; in the verses between he prays about others, first those who seek his life, then all who seek God.

members.words: Hurry, O LORD, to help me!
May those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded;
May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You;
You are my help and my deliverer;

structures.evidence: Boys reads the whole psalm as four members, the fourth answering the first and the third the second: in the two outer members the psalmist's prayer refers to himself and he speaks of help, in the two inner members it refers to others, his enemies and then his friends.

cites.quote: The whole of the seventieth Psalm is prayer; but there is this distinction: that the prayer of the Psalmist refers, in the two extreme members, A. and A., to himself; and in the two central members, B. and B., to others. ... In both A. and A. he speaks of help. ... his prayer refers to others; that is, to the wicked, or his enemies, in B., and to the righteous, or his friends, in B.

structures.short: Calls to praise, each followed by its reasons
structures.about: Two calls to sing and give glory to the LORD, in verses 1 to 3 and 7 to 12, are each followed by reasons, in verses 4 to 6 and in verse 13: His greatness above all gods, and His coming to judge the earth.

structures.evidence: Boys finds two exhortations, in A and A, supported by two reasons, in B and B: the second exhortation, in the third member, to glorify, to worship and to rejoice in the Lord, corresponds to the first, and the last member, B, gives the reason for it.

cites.quote: Here we have two exhortations in A. and A., supported by two reasons in B. and B. … Then in A. again, the third member, we find a second exhortation, to glorify, to worship, and to rejoice in the Lord; corresponding to the former exhortation, in A. the first member. … And, lastly, we have, in B., the reason for this second exhortation

structures.short: Greetings at both ends; thanks, prayer and urging twice
structures.about: The letter opens and closes with greeting and blessing. Between them come two long parts, 1:3 to 2:12 and 2:13 to 3:15, and each gives thanks, then prays, then urges the readers, in the same order.

members.words: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

But we should always thank God for you, brothers
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you.

structures.evidence: Boys reads the whole epistle as an introverted parallelism of four members. The first and last are epistolary; the two central members have three parts each, thanksgiving, prayer and admonition, which answer each other in the order they stand.

cites.at: Part I, the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians, p. 21
cites.quote: Its general character is that of an introverted parallelism of four members, A. B. B. A. ... The two extreme members, A. and A., are epistolary ... The two central members, B. and B., consist of three parts each, which parts correspond respectively in the order in which they stand. The following is a skeleton of the Epistle ... Thanksgiving. ... Prayer. ... Admonition.

structures.evidence: Boys divides two members of 2 Peter into three parts each, which correspond in turn, the first to the first, the second to the second and the third to the third: Peter himself; the apostles and prophets more generally; and the wicked, who are exposed and denounced.

structures.short: Exhortation at both ends, teaching in the middle

structures.evidence: Boys sets out 1 Thessalonians 4:1-5:22 as an introverted parallelism of four members, the last answering to the first and the third to the second: one pair hortatory, where the Apostle exhorts to various duties, and the other didactic, where he instructs on two points.
